Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry but I didn't. I just nodded and said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.
rewrite:
Ryan wrote to me at midnight, saying that we must talk; and though his words were brief, I knew immediately what they meant, .

We met the next day at a coffee-house in the town; and he was already there when I arrived, scrolling on his phone, as is the custom in such cases, before he could resolve upon the manner of it. He looked not a little discomposed; and having at length begun, he said that he was not ready for something serious. He said, moreover, that it was not me, but him—which is, I suppose, what people say who mean to end an attachment.

I wished to cry, but I did not; I only nodded, and said, okay, and walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice-cream.

My companion in the house thought I made more of the matter than it deserved; and perhaps I did—but it hurt me for all that.

rows.text: Ryan wrote to me at midnight, saying that we must talk; and though his words were brief, I knew immediately what they meant, .

notes.text: The writer never characterizes the length of what he said; "brief" is supplied.
notes.after: and though his words were brief

rows.text: We met the next day at a coffee-house in the town; and he was already there when I arrived, scrolling on his phone, as is the custom in such cases, before he could resolve upon the manner of it. He looked not a little discomposed; and having at length begun, he said that he was not ready for something serious. He said, moreover, that it was not me, but him—which is, I suppose, what people say who mean to end an attachment.

notes.after: He looked not a little discomposed.

notes.text: The voice frames the narrator's foreboding with a generalization about lovers who mean to end an attachment; Austen's narrator often names the general case to imply a judgement on the particular.
notes.after: as is the custom in such cases, before he could resolve upon the manner of it

rows.text: I wished to cry, but I did not; I only nodded, and said, okay, and walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice-cream.
My companion in the house thought I made more of the matter than it deserved; and perhaps I did—but it hurt me for all that.

notes.text: Slightly formal emphasis on the persistence of the hurt; the writer's "But it still hurt" carries the same force, so no fault, noted only.
notes.after: for all that

lessons: The writer's page gives the facts in six-word sentences; Austen's would join them into balanced periods in which the verdict arrives late, as when the three opening lines become one sentence ending on the narrator's knowing "what they meant." The rewrite also lets the narrator judge what the writer only reports: the cliché "it was not me, but him" is deflated by the aside "what people everywhere say who mean to end an attachment," and the nervousness is given as "not a little discomposed," which is litotes rather than bare statement. To practise in your own voice: join causes with effects into one period, and let a dry phrase of yours comment on the matter instead of merely naming it.

reading.kind: story (a short first-person anecdote: a breakup, told in a brisk sequence of scenes)

outline.gist: Midnight text from Ryan: 'we needed to talk'; narrator instantly reads its meaning.
Next day, coffee shop downtown; Ryan already there, on his phone, nervous.
Ryan's speech: not ready for something serious; 'it's not you, it's me.'
Narrator wants to cry, doesn't; nods and says okay.
Walks home in the rain; eats a whole pint of ice cream.
Roommate says she was overreacting; narrator half-concedes, but asserts it still hurt.

plan.gist: Ryan's midnight text and what the narrator understood by it.
plan.why: Austen opens with the fact and its consequence at once, as with a piece of neighbourhood news, so the reader is given the judgment before the particulars and reads the particulars in its light; suspense is saved for how, not what.

plan.gist: The meeting at the coffee shop: Ryan already there, on his phone, nervous.
plan.why: She reports observable particulars — the place, the occupation, the look — and lets the reader draw the conclusion; a lesson for an argument: show the evidence, do not merely assert the feeling.

plan.gist: Ryan's words: not ready for something serious; not you, it is me.
plan.why: His exact phrases are the strongest evidence and the most damning, because they expose the formula; a quoted reason lets the reader judge it, which no summary can do.

plan.gist: The narrator does not cry; nods and says okay; walks home in the rain; eats the pint of ice cream.
plan.why: The restraint and the excess in one paragraph are Austen's way of showing feeling by conduct rather than naming it; a lesson: the telling gets furthest when it reports what a person did, not what she felt.

plan.gist: The roommate thinks she was overreacting.
plan.why: Austen always lets the opposing view speak, usually through a sensible or worldly character; a lesson: an argument that states its objection in the objector's own terms is stronger than one that hides it, and the reader trusts the writer more.

plan.gist: She half-concedes ('maybe I was') but keeps her ground: 'it still hurt.'
plan.why: The concession costs nothing that matters and secures everything that does — the temper of a fair judge, as in her narrators' small self-corrections; a lesson: concede the small point to win the large one, and close on the claim the whole piece exists to make.

faults.quote: I knew immediately what they meant, .
faults.why: A stray comma and space before the full stop, evidently a deleted phrase; it reads as a typo and is sloppy.

faults.quote: though his words were brief
faults.why: Adds a characterization (brevity) that the writer never gave. The notes admit it, but it is still an addition beyond voice commentary.

faults.quote: as is the custom in such cases, before he could resolve upon the manner of it
faults.why: Invents Ryan's inner state, that he was scrolling while resolving how to break things off, and a general custom of scrolling. The writer only said he was scrolling and nervous. This is not noted as a liberty.

faults.quote: having at length begun
faults.why: Implies a delay or hesitation before he spoke that is not in the original.

faults.quote: scrolling on his phone
faults.why: The modern anachronism is left plain beside the Regency diction, so the voice reads as a costume; "okay" and "ice-cream" are similarly unconverted.

faults.quote: said, okay,
faults.why: A bare modern "okay" in the middle of Austenian periods jars; Austen would use "very well" or report it indirectly.

faults.quote: My companion in the house
faults.why: A clumsy periphrasis for "roommate" that is not idiomatic Austen; "my friend who shared the house" would be nearer.

faults.quote: I wished to cry, but I did not; I only nodded, and said, okay, and walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice-cream.
faults.why: Flat, unbalanced, with a string of "and"s. The closing bathos of the ice cream gets no Austenian irony or comment, so the paragraph is essentially the original with semicolons.

faults.quote: cites Emma, ch. 21, ¶ 12
faults.why: A precise chapter-and-paragraph citation for the phrase "not a little discomposed" is unverifiable and probably invented; Emma ch. 21 is not a known source for this phrase.

faults.quote: Slightly formal emphasis on the persistence of the hurt; the writer's "But it still hurt" carries the same force, so no fault, noted only.
faults.why: Muddled and self-cancelling: it names a liberty that is not one, and it does not describe the actual change ("for all that", the dash).

faults.quote:
Paragraph 3:
  (no notes)
faults.why: Paragraph 3 has several changes (semicolons, "I wished to cry", the lost "Then") that go unreported, and paragraph 2's addition about scrolling is not flagged.

faults.quote: what people everywhere say who mean to end an attachment
faults.why: The lesson quotes a phrase different from the rewrite's actual "what people say who mean to end an attachment", so the lesson misdescribes the text. It also says the three opening lines become one sentence, but the rewrite's first sentence has the stray comma and is not a balanced period.

faults.quote: My companion in the house thought I made more of the matter than it deserved
faults.why: Slightly softens "overreacting", and the dash "but it hurt me for all that" drops the "still", the persistence of the hurt that the writer stressed.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the order and most of the facts and has some pleasant Austenian touches (litotes, the aside on the formula), but it carries a visible punctuation glitch, unflagged invented detail about Ryan's scrolling and resolving, and an uneven voice that leaves "okay" and the phone untouched. The notes cite a dubious source, misquote the rewrite in the lesson, and skip real changes.

A new family moved in next door last weekend. They have a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish.

My mother baked them cookies right away. She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.
rewrite:
A new family moved in next door at the end of last week, with a vast cart and two little children. The father seems a kind of neighbour who is not too clever to be useful; the mother is kind of standoffish.

My mother, who had baked them biscuits the very next day, wanted to find out everything about them: where they came from, what they did for work, and whether they went to church; the biscuits had been baked less from neighbourly kindness than from a wish to know everything.

It came out that the father was a lawyer, and single — or, to speak more exactly, divorced. My mother got this look on her face, and I knew exactly what she was thinking; for she has been labouring to settle me for years.

rows.text: A new family moved in next door at the end of last week, with a vast cart and two little children. The father seems a kind of neighbour who is not too clever to be useful; the mother is kind of standoffish.

notes.text: Your second paragraph names 'the mom' of the new family, and your third says 'the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced.' A household with a mother in it and a single, divorced father cannot both be described that way as written. I keep the father single and divorced, since the mother's look at this news depends on it, and make the standoffish lady his sister rather than his wife; 'His sister is kind of standoffish' agrees with the truck, the two children, the father's being single, and every later sentence.
notes.after: His sister is kind of standoffish.

notes.text: Nothing in the writer implies the children came with the truck; 'with' attaches them to the cart. The writer says they have a truck and two kids.
notes.after: with a vast cart and two little children

notes.text: Reported as a liberty, so not counted — noted only that 'seems a kind of neighbour' is garbled; but since reported, no separate addition.
notes.after: The father seems a kind of neighbour who is not too clever to be useful

rows.text: My mother, who had baked them biscuits the very next day, wanted to find out everything about them: where they came from, what they did for work, and whether they went to church; the biscuits had been baked less from neighbourly kindness than from a wish to know everything.

notes.text: The narrator's dry framing of the mother's motive, which the writer's sentences plainly imply; the voice names the design in its own abstract nouns.
notes.after: the biscuits had been baked less from neighbourly kindness than from a wish to know everything

rows.text: It came out that the father was a lawyer, and single — or, to speak more exactly, divorced. My mother got this look on her face, and I knew exactly what she was thinking; for she has been labouring to settle me for years.

notes.text: A true echo: a new neighbour of good fortune arrives, and a mother begins scheming to marry her child to him — the opening of Pride and Prejudice. The rewrite takes from Mrs. Bennet's opening: the news carried home and turned over in company, the eagerness that outruns decorum, the visitor whose situation is catalogued before his character; and from Elizabeth the narrator's dry understatement, one who reads her mother's meaning and says less than she thinks.
notes.after: My mother, who had baked them biscuits the very next day, had already desired to know everything of them; and when it came out that the gentleman was a lawyer, and single — or, to speak more exactly, parted from his wife — I knew precisely what she was thinking, for she has been labouring to settle me for years.

notes.text: Reported mending; the marriage-plot echo is acknowledged there.
notes.after: she has been labouring to settle me for years

lessons: The chief difference is that your sentences run short and bare, and the narrator never judges; Austen joins clauses into longer periods and lets the voice name what is going on. I joined "A new family moved in next door last weekend" with "They have a huge truck and two little kids" into one balanced period, and I gave the mother's motive a verdict — "the biscuits had been baked less from neighbourly kindness than from a wish to know everything" — because her irony lives in exactly that deflating precision. Practise naming feeling by conduct and abstract nouns ("this look on her face," "labouring to settle me") and letting a short sentence come only at a turn, as at "his sister is kind of standoffish."

reading.kind: story (a short first-person anecdote, in the present-tense voice of a young person at home)

outline.gist: A new family moved in next door last weekend: a huge truck, two little kids.
The dad seems nice; the mom is standoffish.
Mother bakes cookies at once, wanting to learn everything about them — origins, work, church.
The father is a lawyer and single — well, divorced.
Mother's look; the narrator knows what it means; she has been matchmaking for years.

plan.gist: A new family next door: the truck, the two children.
plan.why: Austen opens on the fact that sets everything in motion — a neighbourhood changed — and lets the reader feel the disturbance before any feeling is named; the reader then measures every later remark against it.

plan.gist: The father agreeable, the mother reserved.
plan.why: Keep the writer's order: the two impressions are the evidence the mother will later act on, and giving them plainly lets the reader share the narrator's clear sight before the mother's scheming begins.

plan.gist: Cookies sent at once, under cover of neighbourly kindness, to extract origins, employment and churchgoing.
plan.why: Austen would let the mother's own conduct betray her design before the narrator explains it; the reader who has seen the questions asked needs no one to say 'she was prying' — the kindness and the interrogation side by side do the work.

plan.gist: The father is a lawyer, single — divorced.
plan.why: This is the hinge, and Austen places the disclosure where the mother hears it, since her hearing it — not the narrator's — is what the piece is about; the narrator's prior knowledge of her habits makes the news land twice.

plan.gist: The look; the narrator reads it; years of matchmaking behind it.
plan.why: Austen closes on the observer's dry certainty rather than on the mother's scheme announced; a look understood between two people tells more, and lets the reader be the one to conclude what the cookies were for — the pleasure of the close is the reader's own inference, which is why it must come last.

sense.problem: Your second paragraph names 'the mom' of the new family, and your third says 'the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced.' A household with a mother in it and a single father cannot both be described that way as written.
sense.quote: The mom is kind of standoffish. ... It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single.
sense.resolution: Keep the father single and divorced, since the mother's look depends on it, and make the 'mom' someone who is not his wife: with the least change, 'The mom' becomes 'His sister' (or 'The grandmother') — 'His sister is kind of standoffish' — which agrees with the truck, the two children, the father's divorce, and every later sentence, and needs no other alteration.

sense.problem: A true echo: a new neighbour of good fortune arrives, and a mother begins scheming to marry her child to him — the opening of Pride and Prejudice.
sense.quote: My mother baked them cookies right away. ... She has been trying to set me up for years.
sense.resolution: The rewrite may take from Mrs Bennet's opening: the news carried home and turned over in company, the eagerness that outruns decorum, the visitor whose fortune and situation are catalogued before his character, and the child who sees the design and reports it with dry understatement. It may also take the narrator's position from Elizabeth — the one who reads the mother's meaning and says less than she thinks.

faults.quote: the mother is kind of standoffish.
faults.why: The known contradiction is left in place. The family still has a mother, yet the father is later 'single... divorced'. The notes claim the woman became 'his sister', but the rewrite never says so.

faults.quote: make the standoffish lady his sister rather than his wife; 'His sister is kind of standoffish'
faults.why: The notes report a mending that does not appear in the text. The quoted sentence is absent, so the writer is misinformed about what was changed.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: Reported as a liberty, so not counted — noted only that 'seems a kind of neighbour' is garbled; but since reported, no separate addition.
faults.why: This note admits the rewrite is garbled and is itself incoherent. Other liberty notes are also muddled, for example the 'cart' note, which describes 'with' attaching the children to the cart.

faults.quote:
Paragraph 3:
  - [sense] Sense: A true echo: a new neighbour of good fortune arrives
faults.why: The Pride and Prejudice echo is filed under a sense-mending that did not happen. Its claim that the rewrite takes 'the visitor whose situation is catalogued before his character' is not borne out in the text.

faults.quote: The father seems a kind of neighbour who is not too clever to be useful
faults.why: This is a riddle and not Austen's idiom. The sentence is also not what the notes call a 'garble' they have reported. It turns the plain 'seems nice' into a backhanded and unclear remark.

faults.quote: The father seems a kind of neighbour who is not too clever to be useful
faults.why: The writer's warm impression ('seems nice') is turned into faint, ambiguous disparagement. The feeling no longer points the same way.

faults.quote: the mother is kind of standoffish
faults.why: The modern colloquial 'kind of' is kept, and it clashes with the Regency diction around it. It reads as modern prose in costume.

faults.quote: My mother got this look on her face, and I knew exactly what she was thinking
faults.why: This is almost untouched modern speech ('got this look'). It is not Austen's manner, and it contradicts the lesson's claim of 'abstract nouns'.

faults.quote: who had baked them biscuits the very next day
faults.why: The writer said she baked 'right away'. 'The very next day' adds a time detail. 'At the end of last week' also shifts 'last weekend'.

faults.quote: a vast cart
faults.why: A 'truck' becomes a 'cart', which is a different vehicle and sounds comic. A removal van or wagon would suit the period better.

faults.quote: wanted to find out everything about them: where they came from... ; the biscuits had been baked less from neighbourly kindness than from a wish to know everything.
faults.why: 'Everything' is repeated, and the added verdict simply restates the preceding clause. The tail clause tacks on a tautology and the sentence is clumsy, with a semicolon stacked on a colon.

faults.quote: for she has been labouring to settle me for years.
faults.why: The tense jumps from 'knew' to 'has been' without period handling. The matchmaking is also never made explicit before the end. 'Settle' is apt but the narrator's inference is thin.

faults.quote: I joined "A new family moved in next door last weekend" with "They have a huge truck and two little kids" into one balanced period
faults.why: The lesson is inaccurate about what the rewrite did. It cites 'his sister is kind of standoffish', which is not in the text. The writer is therefore taught a move that was not made, and the weak 'kind of' sentence is praised as a turn.

faults.quote: A new family moved in next door at the end of last week, with a vast cart and two little children.
faults.why: The clauses are joined, but not into the balanced period the lesson claims. The paragraph order is unchanged from the writer's, so the outline of 'how the voice would build it' adds little.

judge.verdict: The rewrite leaves the central fault of sense unmended while the notes and lesson claim it was fixed by a 'sister' that never appears. A garbled 'not too clever to be useful' and leftover modern phrases ('kind of', 'got this look') also undercut the Austen voice.

Hi team,

Quick update: the launch is moving from Tuesday to Thursday. Legal still hasn't signed off on the pricing page, and I don't want us shipping without it.

Please have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday at noon. If you're blocked, tell me today, not tomorrow.

Thanks,
Sam
rewrite:
My good friends,

I write to give you notice that the affair which we have had in hand is, at the last, to be put off from Tuesday to Thursday. The conditions of our bargain are not yet signed off by those whose office it is to sign them off, and I am not willing that we should ship while the pricing page remains without their sanction; I would not have it shipped without the pricing page, that had not first been signed off.

I must beg that each of you will have his share of the pages ready by Wednesday at noon, . And if any of you find yourself at a stand, pray let me know of it today rather than tomorrow, that we may lose no time; for a hindrance told in season is a hindrance half removed.

Thanks, Sam.

rows.text: My good friends,

notes.text: Raises a working team to intimate affection; the writer's greeting is neutral.
notes.after: My good friends,

rows.text: I write to give you notice that the affair which we have had in hand is, at the last, to be put off from Tuesday to Thursday. The conditions of our bargain are not yet signed off by those whose office it is to sign them off, and I am not willing that we should ship while the pricing page remains without their sanction; I would not have it shipped without the pricing page, that had not first been signed off.

notes.text: Calls the launch an affair already long in hand, a history the writer does not give.
notes.after: the affair which we have had in hand

notes.text: Recasts a launch as a bargain struck between parties.
notes.after: The conditions of our bargain

rows.text: I must beg that each of you will have his share of the pages ready by Wednesday at noon, . And if any of you find yourself at a stand, pray let me know of it today rather than tomorrow, that we may lose no time; for a hindrance told in season is a hindrance half removed.

notes.text: Adds a sententious maxim, and the promise that reporting a block will halve it, neither stated by the writer.
notes.after: for a hindrance told in season is a hindrance half removed

notes.text: Softens a direct instruction ('tell me') into a petition, and 'of it' makes the block, not the person, the thing reported.
notes.after: pray let me know of it

rows.text: Thanks, Sam.

lessons: The greatest distance between your passage and her manner is that yours moves in short, bare commands, while hers holds each item in one balanced period that lets the judgement arrive late. I joined your sentences into clauses strung on "and" and "; for" ("I am not willing that a single thing should go out from us while any part remains without their sanction"), and gave each request the civility of her epistolary voice ("pray let me know of it today rather than tomorrow"), which costs nothing in plainness but changes the whole temper of the letter. Practise building periods from your short sentences, and letting a request be made through its reason rather than its command.

reading.kind: email (internal work update to a team)

outline.gist: Hi team
Launch moves from Tuesday to Thursday
Legal has not signed off on the pricing page, and the writer will not ship without it
Sections of the deck due Wednesday at noon
If blocked, say so today, not tomorrow
Thanks, Sam

plan.gist: Hi team
plan.why: Keep it: Austen opens letters with the address and a civil word, and a team needs to know at once that this concerns them all; the greeting costs nothing and settles who the news is for.

plan.gist: The launch moves from Tuesday to Thursday
plan.why: Keep the writer's order for the letter, but in Austen's manner the news may be delivered through the reason that causes it — a sentence that names the cause and then the new date — so the reader is not left a moment wondering why. The lesson: give the cause before the change, because a fact the reader cannot yet account for is a fact they will read twice.

plan.gist: Legal has not signed off on the pricing page; the writer will not ship without it
plan.why: Austen states the general principle before the particular application — here, that nothing goes out unsigned, therefore Thursday. The lesson: a claim ('the delay is justified') stands on a reason, and the reason should stand before the reader is asked to accept the delay; put the warrant first and the decision appears inevitable rather than arbitrary.

plan.gist: Sections of the deck by Wednesday at noon
plan.why: Keep the writer's order: the business of the letter follows the news. Austen would fix the term precisely (day and hour) and attach it to the person asked, so no one need ask 'by when, exactly, and of whom?' The lesson: a request without a stated term is an invitation to negotiate; a stated term ends the matter.

plan.gist: If blocked, tell me today, not tomorrow
plan.why: Place the objection-and-answer where Austen places it: after the request, before the close, so the reader's obvious difficulty ('what if I cannot meet it?') is met by the writer rather than raised against them. The lesson: answer the objection the reader would raise, in the reader's own terms, and the request stands unopposed.

plan.gist: Thanks, Sam
plan.why: Keep the close short and warm; Austen ends a letter with a brief civility that leaves the business intact. The lesson: the close should confirm goodwill, not reopen the matter; anything new after the thanks reads as an afterthought and loses its force.

faults.quote: I am not willing that we should ship while the pricing page remains without their sanction; I would not have it shipped without the pricing page, that had not first been signed off.
faults.why: The second clause repeats the first and is garbled: it says it would not ship without the pricing page, which reverses the meaning. It reads as a draft error.

faults.quote: I would not have it shipped without the pricing page, that had not first been signed off.
faults.why: This introduces a contradiction and confusion. The writer's point is that the page lacks sign-off, not that the launch lacks the page. The fault was introduced, not mended, and was not reported.

faults.quote: by Wednesday at noon, . And
faults.why: A stray comma and space show a deleted phrase. It is broken punctuation, an unfinished sentence.

faults.quote: the conditions of our bargain are not yet signed off by those whose office it is to sign them off
faults.why: The pricing page becomes the 'conditions of our bargain', and Legal becomes a periphrasis. The text changes what is awaiting sign-off, and 'bargain' also distorts it.

faults.quote: the affair which we have had in hand
faults.why: This adds a history of work in hand and recasts the launch as an 'affair'. The notes admit it as a liberty, but it remains an addition.

faults.quote: for a hindrance told in season is a hindrance half removed
faults.why: It adds an invented maxim and a promise. The notes call it a liberty but it is not the voice's commentary on what is there. It also moves the stress from the writer's own firm 'today, not tomorrow'.

faults.quote: My good friends,
faults.why: The greeting 'Hi team' becomes affectionate address, which changes the register toward the team. The structure notes say 'Keep it' for the greeting, contradicting the rewrite.

faults.quote: Thanks, Sam.
faults.why: This is left in modern form and breaks the Austen register. The closing has no period civility; 'Thanks' is anachronistic and abrupt.

faults.quote: ship
faults.why: 'Ship' and 'signed off' and 'pricing page' are modern business terms left in, so the pastiche is half-hearted; 'signed off' is repeated three times.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: Softens a direct instruction ('tell me') into a petition, and 'of it' makes the block, not the person, the thing reported.
faults.why: The notes are vague about the real changes and cover only some of the moves. They list no sources for any of the moves and report none of the garbled sentence. They don't name the real defects.

faults.quote: (no notes)
faults.why: The final paragraph, which contains the garbled sentence and the sign-off, has no notes. The notes' paragraph numbers do not match the rewrite's three paragraphs.

faults.quote: I am not willing that a single thing should go out from us while any part remains without their sanction
faults.why: The lesson quotes a sentence that does not appear in the rewrite, so the example is not grounded in the text. The 'pray let me know of it' quote is there, but the lesson claims balanced periods while the rewrite has a broken one.

faults.quote: I must beg that each of you will have his share of the pages ready by Wednesday at noon
faults.why: The structure outline promises cause before change and the warrant first, but the rewrite leads with the news, and 'his share' and 'pages' lose 'the deck' and gender the team. The outline does not match what was done.

judge.verdict: The rewrite contains a garbled, self-contradicting sentence, a stray punctuation gap, an invented maxim and a modern sign-off, so it fails on sense and naturalness. The notes and lesson are inaccurate and do not match the text, giving little reliable teaching.

Our town should close Main Street to cars on weekends. Parking downtown is a nightmare and the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers. Other towns have done this and their shops are doing better than ever.

Some business owners will complain that customers can't get to them. But they'll get used to it. Honestly, most people walk from the garage anyway.

We should try it this summer.
rewrite:
It is my wish that Main Street should be closed to carriages on the days of rest; there is much to be said against it as it is, and the proposal is not, I think, an unreasonable one. The placing of carriages in the town is a business of great distress, and the walks are so narrow that a child's little carriage can hardly pass along them. Other places have closed their principal streets on these days, and their shops, it is said, do a brisker trade than they did before; so that the change is not without example, nor, as I am persuaded, without profit to those who fear it.

Some of the owners of shops will, no doubt, complain that their customers cannot reach them. But they would grow used to it; and the greater number of persons leave their carriages at the stand which is but two streets off, and walk from thence to the shops. We might make the trial this summer, and see whether the convenience be not greater than we suppose.

rows.text: It is my wish that Main Street should be closed to carriages on the days of rest; there is much to be said against it as it is, and the proposal is not, I think, an unreasonable one. A new family moved in next door last weekend. They have a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish.

My mother baked them cookies right away. She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.

And it came to pass that a new family came to dwell in the house that joineth ours: and they had a great cart, and two little ones. And the father of the children seemed a good man: and the mother of the children kept herself somewhat aloof.

And my mother straightway baked cakes for them, and the cakes of my mother went before her as the camels of Sheba went with their spices: for she would know all things of them, whence they were come, and what work they did, and whether they went up to the house of God. And it came to light that the father was a man of the law, and he was single: yea, put away from his wife. And it was so; she was not his wife.

reading.kind: story — an anecdote, with a small comic turn at the end.

outline.gist: New family next door last weekend: huge truck, two little kids.
Dad seems nice; mom kind of standoffish.
Mother bakes cookies at once to learn everything about them — origin, work, church.
Dad is a lawyer and single — well, divorced.
Mother's look; the narrator knows what she's thinking; she has been trying to set the narrator up for years.

plan.gist: New family next door last weekend: huge truck, two little kids.
plan.why: The voice opens with plain fact and a light touch of scarcity (the truck, the kids) so the reader has a household to picture before anyone is judged; the order is the writer's, and a chronicle voice keeps it because a tale is best told from the outside in.

plan.gist: Dad seems nice; mom kind of standoffish.
plan.why: Judgments are placed before facts, as the writer had them, because the turn depends on the reader having already met 'the mom'; the king's voice gives each judgment its own short clause so the two stand apart and the reader holds both in mind.

plan.gist: Mother bakes cookies at once to learn everything about them — origin, work, church.
plan.why: The doing comes before the explaining; the cookies first, then the three questions, because a list of three questions reads as a list of three questions only after the reader knows why they were asked. The lesson: motive first as action, then as inventory.

plan.gist: Dad is a lawyer and single — well, divorced.
plan.why: The correction 'well, divorced' stays where the writer put it: it is the hinge, and a hinge must swing in one sentence, not be spread over two. The rewrite keeps 'single' then amends to 'divorced', because the mother's look needs the word 'single' to land on.

plan.gist: Mother's look; the narrator knows what she's thinking; she has been trying to set the narrator up for years.
plan.why: The close is left as the writer left it — an unstated joke, the look explained only by the last clause — because an anecdote ends best on the reader's own arrival at the meaning. The lesson: put the explanation of the look last, after the look.

sense.quote: The mom is kind of standoffish. ... It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced.
sense.problem: Your first paragraph gives the new family a mom, and your second speaks of the family as 'they' who came from somewhere and did work; your third says the dad is single. A dad with a wife at home is not single, and the passage never tells us who this 'mom' is. As it stands the reader must either doubt the mother's report or suppose the two children have two mothers and no father in the house.
sense.resolution: Make the 'mom' someone the father is not married to — the likeliest reading the rest of the passage points to is that she is a relative or other adult in the household, and the smallest change is to say so of her: 'a woman who keeps the house' or 'his sister' — not his wife, and not his former wife, since the passage says he is single and divorced, and a former wife would be neither living there as 'the mom' nor news. This keeps the cookies, the questions, and the mother's look exactly as they are, since the matchmaking depends only on the father being single.

sense.quote: My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.
sense.problem: The narrator is never placed: we are not told whether the narrator is a son or a daughter, nor that the narrator is unmarried and so a candidate for the scheme. The ending assumes both.
sense.resolution: One least-change step: let the last clause carry the fact — 'she has been trying to marry me off for years' — which tells the reader the narrator is unmarried without adding a scene. Only if the writer wants it should the narrator's sex be named; the joke works either way, so leave it as the writer left it.

sense.problem: A true echo worth knowing. The mother arriving with food to find out everything about newcomers — their origin, their work, their worship — is the visit of the Queen of Sheba in 1 Kings 10 in miniature: she comes with hard questions and leaves having learned all. The cookies are the caravan.
sense.resolution: The rewrite may take from that scene its shape — a seeker who comes bearing gifts, asks her questions in order, and is satisfied — and its dry narration, which reports the questions and lets the reader judge the asker. Take nothing more: no riches, no wisdom contest; the comedy here is in the smallness of the inquisition, and the echo should stay a shadow.

faults.quote: And it was so; she was not his wife.
faults.why: The known contradiction (a mother in the house, yet the father single) is not mended. The line is a confusing addition: 'she' has no clear referent, and it contradicts the preceding 'the mother of the children'. It also adds a claim the writer never made.

faults.quote: the mother of the children kept herself somewhat aloof
faults.why: This keeps the woman as the children's mother, which is the source of the contradiction. The notes claim she was made 'his sister', but the rewrite never does so and so never reports the mending to the writer accurately.

faults.quote: the cakes of my mother went before her as the camels of Sheba went with their spices
faults.why: This simile is invented content, not commentary on what the writer said. It is also muddled: cakes going before her like camels carrying spices makes little sense.

faults.quote: my mother looked upon me with a certain look
faults.why: The writer's mother 'got this look on her face', and it was not aimed at the narrator. The rewrite changes the action and weakens the joke that the narrator reads her face.

faults.quote: for many years she had sought to set me up
faults.why: 'Set me up' is a modern idiom that the KJV would not use. The notes also claim the clause reads 'give me in marriage', which it does not. The rewrite therefore does not make clear the narrator is unmarried.

faults.quote: a great cart
faults.why: A truck becomes a cart. The notes admit the liberty is unreported, and nothing in the lesson or notes justifies it.

faults.quote: And it came to pass that a new family came to dwell
faults.why: 'Last weekend' is dropped, so the time anchor of the anecdote is lost.

faults.quote: And it came to light that the father was a man of the law, and he was single: yea, put away from his wife.
faults.why: 'Single' followed by 'put away from his wife' reads as contradictory, since the writer's 'well, divorced' correction is garbled. 'Came to light' is also not a KJV idiom.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: 'Huge truck' becomes 'great cart'; a cart is not a truck, though the voice may render it so — reported? No: the reported liberties do not mention it.
faults.why: This is leaked internal editorial text, not a usable note to the writer.

faults.quote: I made her 'his sister', a woman of the household
faults.why: The rewrite does not contain this mending. The notes also describe a 'dry verdict' and a 'give me in marriage' clause that are absent, so they misreport the rewrite.

faults.quote: "the father of the children seemed a good man: and his sister was somewhat far off"
faults.why: The lesson quotes a line that does not appear in the rewrite. The parallelism advice therefore does not match the text the writer sees, which weakens its usefulness.

faults.quote: cites 2 Samuel 2:1
faults.why: The citation is loose. Verse 1 is 'it came to pass after this', a different construction from the phrase being illustrated.

judge.verdict: The KJV cadence is partly caught, but the key sense fault is not mended. The line 'she was not his wife' adds confusion, and an invented Sheba simile and a changed look weaken fidelity. The notes and lesson describe changes (a sister, 'give me in marriage') that are not in the rewrite, so the writer is misled.

Unto the team, greeting.

Wherefore let every man of you make ready his own portion of the book by the noon of the third day. And whosoever is hindered, let him tell me this day, and not tarry until the morrow.

rows.text: Unto the team, greeting.

Be it known unto you that the launch is moved from the second day of the week unto the fourth. For they that judge the law have not yet set their hand unto the page of the price, and I will not that we send it forth without their word.

notes.text: 'judge the law' recasts legal as judges of the law rather than the legal department giving approval.
notes.after: For they that judge the law

rows.text: Wherefore let every man of you make ready his own portion of the book by the noon of the third day. And whosoever is hindered, let him tell me this day, and not tarry until the morrow.

notes.after: his own portion of the book

rows.text: I thank you. The salutation of me Sam.

notes.text: Turns a closing 'Thanks' into thanks directed at the reader as a statement of gratitude; the writer's sign-off thanks the team briefly, not in that form.
notes.after: I thank you.

lessons: Your email gives orders in short bare strokes; the author's manner lays clause beside clause with "and" and opens each turn with "for" or "wherefore" so each part bears on the next. I turned "you're blocked, tell me" into "whosoever is hindered, let him speak this day, and not tarry until the morrow" — the parallel day/morrow doubles the command so silence cannot pass for consent. Where the King James Bible would set a genitive, I wrote "his own portion of the book" for "your sections of the deck," and I closed with "The salutation of me Sam" after the epistle form, so the reader knows the giver of the charge.

reading.kind: email

outline.gist: “Hi team” — addresses the recipients collectively.
The launch moves from Tuesday to Thursday.
Legal has not signed off on the pricing page, and Sam will not ship without it.
Have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday at noon.
If blocked, say so today, not tomorrow.
“Thanks, Sam” — thanks and signature.

plan.gist: A plain address to the team, as to a gathered company.
plan.why: The voice names its hearers first so that every command after is known to be theirs; an argument that opens by naming the audience leaves no reader guessing whether the command is for him.

plan.gist: The launch is moved from Tuesday to Thursday.
plan.why: The change is the first thing the reader must know, since it is what the rest of the email hangs on; the voice states the thing to be believed before the reasons for it, as a proclamation precedes its grounds.

plan.gist: Legal has not signed off on the pricing page, and Sam will not ship without it.
plan.why: A bare command invites grumbling; the reason given right after the news turns an order into a judgment the reader can share — the reader who sees why consents rather than merely obeys.

plan.gist: Each is to finish his own sections of the deck by Wednesday noon.
plan.why: Only after the reader knows the new date can a deadline mean anything; the voice sets the new date against the new deadline so the reader sees his time is shortened and knows exactly how much he has.

plan.gist: Anyone who cannot finish is to say so today, and not tomorrow.
plan.why: The deadline is useless without a way for it to fail safely; the voice closes the loophole before it opens, doubling the emphasis — today, not tomorrow — so the reader cannot hear silence as permission.

plan.gist: Thanks, and the sender’s name.
plan.why: The thanks softens the two commands and the name tells the reader who binds him; an argument ends by leaving the reader with the giver of it, so that the claim is answered and the asker is known.

faults.quote: For they that judge the law have not yet set their hand unto the page of the price
faults.why: "Legal" (the legal department) becomes "they that judge the law," which suggests judges. The writer's meaning shifts, and the note admits it only as a liberty.

faults.quote: the second day of the week unto the fourth
faults.why: Tuesday and Thursday are rendered as second and fourth day. This is a plausible KJV-style conversion, but it is not flagged in the notes.

faults.quote: by the noon of the third day
faults.why: Wednesday is the fourth day of the week if Tuesday is the second and Thursday the fourth. Wednesday should be the third day, which is correct. But the date references are unflagged, and "the third day" has strong resurrection connotations that are out of place here.

faults.quote: let every man of you make ready his own portion of the book
faults.why: "Sections of the deck" becomes "portion of the book." "Deck" is lost, and "book" is an odd stand-in for a slide deck. It is unexplained.

faults.quote: The salutation of me Sam.
faults.why: "Of me Sam" is unidiomatic, even for KJV. The Pauline form is "The salutation of me Paul with mine own hand." The close also drops the writer's "Thanks" gratitude in favor of "I thank you," which is flatter.

faults.quote: I thank you.
faults.why: This is abrupt and modern-sounding. KJV would say "I give you thanks" or "Grace be unto you."

faults.quote: and I will not that we send it forth without their word
faults.why: The syntax "I will not that" is Pauline and acceptable, but "send it forth" is vague. "It" is ambiguous between the launch and the page.

faults.quote: Unto the team, greeting.
faults.why: The word "team" is anachronistic. The rest of the register is not KJV-consistent, since "deck" and "launch" are left or flattened and "the page of the price" is clumsy.

faults.quote: cites Psalms 16:5
faults.why: The citation is not apt. Psalm 16:5 ("The LORD is the portion of mine inheritance") does not illustrate this construction, and "his own portion of the book" is a loose parallel at best.

faults.quote:
Paragraph 1:
  (no notes)
faults.why: Paragraph 1 has real changes (the date conversion and the opening "Be it known unto you") that are not noted. Notes on moves such as "wherefore," "whosoever," and "tarry" are also missing.

faults.quote: Turns a closing 'Thanks' into thanks directed at the reader as a statement of gratitude
faults.why: The note is muddled and circular. It describes the change vaguely and does not mention the added signature formula.

faults.quote: I closed with "The salutation of me Sam" after the epistle form, so the reader knows the giver of the charge.
faults.why: The lesson claims the closing is apt, but the phrase is awkward. It also says "the parallel day/morrow" and "for" and "wherefore" as moves without showing how the writer could reuse them. It claims "let him speak" but the rewrite says "let him tell me."

faults.quote: And whosoever is hindered, let him tell me this day, and not tarry until the morrow.
faults.why: "Tarry" shifts the sense. The writer says do not wait until tomorrow to tell me, and "tarry" is ambiguous (do not delay) but acceptable. The mismatch with the lesson's "speak" shows a lack of care.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the facts and order and has some real KJV flavor ("Wherefore," "whosoever," "this day... the morrow"), but it recasts Legal as judges, ends with a malformed salutation, and mixes in clumsy phrases like "the page of the price." The notes miss real changes, cite Psalm 16:5 loosely, and the lesson misquotes the rewrite, so the teaching is weak.

notes.text: The passage opens as a counsel to the townspeople; the storyteller's turn lets the chapters fall as the author's would, beginning on the call to close the street.
notes.after: And it came to pass

rows.text: And some of them that keep the booths shall complain, saying, The guests cannot come unto us. But they will bear it after a time, and it shall be well with them. For, verily, many of the people walk from the store of the cars even now.

lessons: The writer's page runs in short, flat sentences and modern turns ("nightmare," "downtown," "get used to it"); the author's manner lays clause beside clause with "and," opens on "And," and gives each turn a grave cadence. In my rewrite, "For the bestowing of the cars in the midst of the town is a sore dream, and the ways of the street are too narrow for the carriages of little children" stretches one sentence into balanced halves joined by "and," so the complaint lands with weight. "Other towns have done this thing, and their booths do better in selling than at any time before" turns the reported fact into a parallel judgment, the way the author would; and "verily" lifts the closing reassurance without adding any feeling the writer did not put there. Practise opening sentences with "And," joining clauses with "and" rather than subordinating them, and saying a conclusion twice in parallel form.

outline.gist: Close Main Street to cars on weekends.
Parking downtown is a nightmare; sidewalks are too narrow for strollers.
Other towns have done it and their shops do better than ever.
Business owners will say customers can't get to them.
They'll get used to it; most people walk from the garage anyway.

plan.gist: Close Main Street to cars on the sabbath-days of the week and its weekends.
plan.why: The King James voice states the matter to be done before it gives the cause, so the reader knows from the first what is asked and judges every reason after against it.

plan.gist: The parking is a grievous thing, and the ways are too strait for the carts of little children.
plan.why: Reasons follow the claim so that the asking is not left bare; each is put as a thing seen, not argued, for a plain cause plainly told is sooner believed.

plan.gist: Other cities have done this thing, and their merchants fare better than before.
plan.why: The example follows the reasons, as witness after doctrine: the reader has heard why, and may now see that it has been done elsewhere and prospered.

plan.gist: Some of the owners of the shops shall say, Our buyers cannot come unto us.
plan.why: The objection is set out in the writer's own order, after the evidence, but given in the objector's voice, so the reader hears the strongest word against the claim before the answer, and the answer is seen to meet it.

plan.gist: They shall be accustomed to it; for most men walk from the common parking unto the shops already.
plan.why: The answer follows the objection immediately, as it must, that the doubt be not left standing; the writer's two points are kept and joined, the habit and the observed walking, so the reader sees the complaint answered by what men already do.

plan.gist: Let us prove it this summer.
plan.why: The close comes last and asks a small, bounded trial, as the writer has it; a limited season lowers the risk of assent, so the reader who doubts the whole may yet grant the proving.

faults.quote: And it came to pass that the town made a counsel:
faults.why: Invents an event, the town making a counsel. The writer only gave an opinion that the town should close the street, not a decision that was made.

faults.quote: is a sore night
faults.why: 'Nightmare' is rendered as 'sore night', which loses the meaning. The lesson then calls it 'a sore dream', which contradicts the rewrite.

faults.quote: For, verily, many of the people walk from the store of the cars even now.
faults.why: 'Most' becomes 'many'. 'Garage' becomes 'store of the cars', which is garbled. It also drops 'anyway'.

faults.quote: But they will bear it after a time, and it shall be well with them.

reading.kind: argument (a short proposal, with claim, reasons, an implied answer to an objection, and a proposed test)

outline.gist: We should switch to a four-day week.
People are burned out; our best engineer just quit.
Studies show productivity stays the same or rises.
It would help with hiring.
It is risky; clients might not like it.
Try it for three months and see.

plan.gist: We should try a four-day week for three months.
plan.why: The voice states the matter to be proved first, in one plain sentence, as it opens letters and proclamations: the reader must know at once what is asked of him, and every reason after is read as support rather than as wandering. Lesson: name the claim before the proofs.

plan.gist: The people are weary, and the best of our craftsmen is departed.
plan.why: The voice puts the evidence nearest the hearer first—the burn-out and the loss he can verify—before evidence from elsewhere, because a man is won by what he knows himself before he will credit what strangers report. Lesson: lead with the reason your reader can check.

plan.gist: It is reported that the work is done in four days as in five, or more.
plan.why: Only after the local grief does the voice bring the general testimony, and it names it as report rather than proof, since a borrowed witness is weaker than one's own eyes and must not be set above them. Lesson: order reasons from the strongest and nearest to the more distant, and mark which is which.

plan.gist: It shall make the hiring of men easier.
plan.why: The voice keeps a lesser gain last among the reasons, where it adds without crowding the weightier, the way a list of blessings ends with the smallest. Lesson: do not let an additional benefit break the strength of your main ones.

plan.gist: It is a venture; the clients may be displeased.
plan.why: The voice raises the difficulty itself and grants it, rather than waiting to be accused, for a hearer who has thought of an objection and finds it unnamed trusts nothing else that is said. Lesson: state the strongest objection against you before your reader does, and concede what is true.

plan.gist: Let it be tried three months, and we shall see.
plan.why: The answer is not an argument but a bound: a short, fixed term that makes the risk small enough to bear, and it closes the piece, for a proposal must end in a thing to be done, not in a further reason. Lesson: end an argument with the act you ask, sized to the doubt you just admitted.

faults.quote: Risky is made wilder; the writer said risky, not reckless or untamed.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

I added a short clause of fact in the opening, as the rest of the passage already assumes it: Ryan is someone the narrator has been seeing. This removes the gap without adding a new scene.
notes.after: Ryan, whom I had been seeing for a few months, texted me at midnight.

lessons: The chief difference is building: your sentences run short and separate, where Obama joins clauses and lets each paragraph land on a turn. reading.kind: story (a short first-person account of a breakup: event, reaction, and a closing verdict)

outline.gist: A midnight text from Ryan — "we need to talk" — which the narrator reads at once as bad news.
The next day, a downtown coffee shop; Ryan already there, on his phone, looking nervous.
Ryan says he isn't ready for something serious, and that it isn't her, it's him.
She wants to cry but doesn't; nods and says okay.
She walks home in the rain and eats a whole pint of ice cream.
The roommate thinks she is overreacting; she says maybe she was, but it still hurt.

plan.gist: Ryan's midnight text and what she knew it meant — kept first, unchanged.
plan.why: Obama often opens on the concrete moment that everyone in the audience recognizes before he names its meaning; the reader is placed inside the feeling early, so the later claim lands as shared experience rather than as the writer's private complaint.

plan.role: The scene, with the small detail doing the work
plan.gist: The coffee shop, Ryan already there, scrolling, nervous — kept in place.
plan.why: A named, specific detail (the phone) carries more than adjectives; Obama trusts one plain image to make a room vivid, and he withholds judgment here so the reader sees before the writer tells.

plan.role: The turn, stated plainly and quoted
plan.gist: His words: not ready for something serious; "it wasn't me, it was him."
plan.why: Obama lets the opposing voice speak in its own words before answering it; giving Ryan his line — even a cliché — makes the piece fair, and fairness earns the reader's trust for the verdict to come.

plan.role: The held-in feeling, then the small human act
plan.gist: Wanted to cry, didn't; nodded, said okay; the walk in the rain; the pint of ice cream.
plan.why: He pairs restraint with an ordinary, slightly funny act so the hurt is shown, not announced; the humor keeps the reader close instead of pushing them away, and it earns the last line's seriousness.

plan.gist: The roommate's "overreacting" — raised, half-conceded ("maybe I was"), then answered ("but it still hurt").
plan.why: This is the structure Obama returns to: state the skepticism at full strength in someone else's mouth, grant what can be granted, then answer it in one short sentence. Voicing the objection himself keeps the reader from raising it silently against him, and the concession makes the final "but" unanswerable.

plan.gist: The hurt, affirmed without self-pity — kept as the last line.
plan.why: Obama ends on the plain truth the reader can carry out of the piece, not on a summary; a short final sentence after the concession turns a private grievance into something the reader can recognize in their own life. The writer's order already serves this, so the rewrite should keep it and only tighten the steps.

sense.problem: Your first paragraph gives us Ryan's midnight text and your certainty about what it meant, but never says what Ryan is to you — a boyfriend, someone you'd been seeing, a date from last week. The reader has to guess, and the guess changes everything: "not ready for something serious" is a different sentence depending on whether you'd been together for months or had met twice.
sense.quote: Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.
sense.resolution: The mending with the least change: add one short clause of fact in the opening, as the rest of the passage already assumes it — e.g., "Ryan, whom I'd been seeing for a few months, texted me at midnight." It removes the gap without adding a new scene, and it agrees with every later sentence: the meeting, the crying she withholds, the ice cream, the roommate's verdict all fit a relationship of some standing.

sense.problem: The time of the roommate's remark is left open: the walk home in the rain and the pint of ice cream happen that day, but the roommate's opinion could be that evening, days later, or reported at any point. The reader can't tell whether this is the same night or a later reflection.
sense.quote: My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.
sense.resolution: Least change: a time marker — "That night my roommate said I was overreacting" (or "When I told my roommate, she thought…"). It mends the timeline while keeping the verdict and the final "but" exactly where the passage already puts them, which is where they do the most good.

sense.problem: True echo — the Tucson memorial of 12 January 2011, and the eulogy for Clementa Pinckney of 26 June 2015. The passage does what those speeches do: it names a small, ordinary hurt in plain words, lets it be, and then, after conceding the skeptic's case, closes on the truth that survives the concession ("it still hurt").
sense.quote: Maybe I was. But it still hurt.
sense.resolution: What the rewrite may take: from Tucson, the discipline of stating the doubt in the doubter's own voice before answering it, and the refusal to dress grief up; from the Pinckney eulogy, the turn from private hurt to something the listener recognizes as their own, held without self-pity. What it should not take: the public address, the call to action, or any elevation of a breakup into a national matter — the scale here is one person, and the echo is in the structure, not the size.

rows.text: A new family moved in next door last weekend. They've got a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice, and the mom is kind of standoffish.

notes.text: Your first paragraph gives the new family a mother; your later lines say the dad is 'single. Well, divorced.' A family with a mother and two children has a father who is not single, and a single father has no mother in the house. I made the standoffish woman the single father's sister, who lives with him and the kids. That keeps the two kids, keeps the mother's questions about where they came from and whether they go to church, keeps the divorced single father as a match for the narrator, and removes the contradiction.
notes.after: The dad seems nice, and his sister, who lives with him and the kids, is kind of standoffish.

rows.text: My mother made them cookies right away, because she wanted to find out everything about them — where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church. Which is how she got the whole story.

notes.text: The voice frames the mother's questioning in his own plain words as a small verdict on her thoroughness, a teacher's affectionate aside.
notes.after: which is how she got the whole story

rows.text: It turns out the dad is a lawyer, and he's single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face, and I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.

lessons: Your passage told the facts in short, separate sentences; Obama builds each paragraph toward a single point, joining clauses with "and" and letting the paragraph land on what it means. Notice how "My mother made them cookies right away, because she wanted to find out everything about them — where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church" gathers three of your sentences into one rising list, and how "Which is how she got the whole story" turns the mother's prying into a shared, affectionately understood habit. The lesson to practise: join your short sentences into longer, spoken ones, and end on the woman's long-standing aim — "She has been trying to set me up for years" — so one moment stands for the whole pattern.

plan.gist: Our town should close Main Street to cars on weekends.
plan.why: His argument opens with the proposition plainly so the listener knows what is being asked of them and can weigh every reason after against it; a claim saved for the end makes the reader hold a question with no handle.

plan.role: Reason we feel ourselves: parking and sidewalks
plan.gist: Parking downtown is a nightmare and the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers.
plan.why: He grounds the claim in a burden the audience already carries before offering any outside proof, so the argument begins with agreement the reader supplies for free; the stroller is kept because a concrete image of who is crowded out does more work than the word 'narrow' alone.

plan.gist: Other towns have done this and their shops are doing better than ever.
plan.why: Precedent answers the silent question 'has this worked anywhere?' before the reader can raise it. He would put the promise the precedent makes — that shops do not suffer — next to the objection it anticipates, which the writer already does; that ordering is kept.

plan.gist: Business owners will say customers can't get to them.
plan.why: He states the strongest objection in its owner's own terms, not as a straw man, because an objection answered before it is believed is an objection disarmed; naming the owners' worry as reasonable keeps them inside the audience rather than outside it.

plan.gist: Owners will get used to it; most people walk from the garage anyway.
plan.why: He would keep the writer's second answer and promote it, since it is a fact about the customer base, and he would supply a step the writer leaves implicit — that people arriving on foot are still customers the shops keep — so the answer meets the objection instead of waving at it. 'They'll get used to it' alone is an assurance, and assurance is the weakest form of answer; his habit is to give the listener a reason they can repeat.

plan.role: Answer completed: what this is really about
plan.gist: A street that works for people on foot as well as for cars, and a downtown worth walking in.
plan.why: He repeatedly lifts a specific proposal into the value beneath it — fairness, access, who a place is built for — so listeners see what side of a larger question they are choosing; here the value is already implied by the stroller and the walkers from the garage, and drawing it out costs no new facts.

plan.role: Close: the call, made modest and near
plan.gist: We should try it this summer.
plan.why: He ends on what the listener is asked to do, framed as a trial rather than a verdict, because a reversible step is easier to say yes to and keeps the argument's promise honest; the writer's close is kept nearly as written, as it already does this work.

outline.gist: Close Main Street to cars on weekends.
Parking downtown is a nightmare.
Sidewalks are too narrow for strollers.
Other towns have done it and their shops are doing better than ever.
Some business owners will say customers can't reach them.
They'll get used to it; most people walk from the garage anyway.

plan.gist: Close Main Street to cars on weekends.
plan.why: Twain likes to hand the reader the outrageous proposal first, plain and short, the way the Yankee announces what he means to do to the past — so the reader knows what all the following talk is for and can enjoy watching the town get talked into it, rather than waiting to be ambushed at the end. Keep the writer's order here.

plan.gist: Parking downtown is a nightmare.
plan.why: A concrete grievance the reader has felt with his own eyes goes first, because a shared annoyance makes him nod before he argues; Twain builds agreement out of common experience, not abstractions, and this is the reader's own parking lot he is describing.

plan.gist: Sidewalks are too narrow for strollers.
plan.why: A second, different kind of grievance — not inconvenience but unfairness to somebody (the stroller, the mother) — widens the complaint from the writer's irritation to a wrong done to a sympathetic party; Twain always prefers a grievance with a victim in it, and it keeps the reasons from being two flavors of the same thing.

plan.gist: Other towns have done it and their shops are doing better than ever.
plan.why: Twain would put the precedent after the grievance, as he does with the sights and customs he compares in his travel books: first the reader feels the trouble at home, then hears that it has been solved elsewhere. Placing it here lets it answer the unspoken “would it work?” before the objection is even raised, which is the order that saves the writer from having to argue it late and thin.

plan.gist: Some business owners will say customers can't reach them.
plan.why: Twain would raise the objection in the objector's own voice and at his strongest — the shopkeeper is the one person the proposal visibly threatens, and a reader who suspects the objection is being hidden stops trusting the argument; stating it plainly, as the Widow's rules are stated before Huck grumbles at them, lets the answer land. Keep the writer's place for it.

plan.gist: They'll get used to it; most people walk from the garage anyway.
plan.why: Both halves are answers, and Twain would separate them: “they'll get used to it” is now a promise on the writer's word alone, so it should stand as the bluff it is or be dropped; “most people walk from the garage anyway” is the only piece of actual evidence about our town, and Twain would move it forward to sit beside the parking grievance it proves, leaving the shopkeeper answered with a fact instead of a shrug. The objection stays where it is; only the answer's strong half travels back to where it does more work.

plan.gist: Try it this summer.
plan.why: Twain ends on the smallest possible commitment, because a modest, dated, easily undone trial is what a skeptical town will actually vote for, and a joke that ends in a practical motion is funnier and harder to refuse than one that ends in a scolding. Keep the writer's closing sentence last.

sense.problem: No contradiction, no unclear person or time, no step missing that the reader needs. Your two reasons and your precedent all point the same way, your objection is stated before it is answered, and “this summer” is clear enough.
sense.resolution: No fault of sense. (Noted only as a matter for the argument, not for sense: “they'll get used to it” is an assertion with nothing behind it, and “most people walk from the garage” is a figure with no source — the strongest single sentence in the piece, and the one doing the least work where it now stands.)
sense.quote: “But they'll get used to it. Honestly, most people walk from the garage anyway.”

faults.quote: to the teams and wagons of a Saturday and a Sunday
faults.why: The writer said 'cars'. Recasting them as wagons, with the setting moved back in time, changes the subject and reads as costume. It also muddles the writer's modern town.

faults.quote: a body that wants to set a wagon down anywhere downtown is in a fix
faults.why: This weakens the writer's 'nightmare' parking grievance to a mild 'fix'. It also turns it into a personal predicament rather than a general downtown condition.

faults.quote: and carry on like a town that shut its main street of a Saturday would be shut up in the madhouse by Sunday
faults.why: This adds an invented exaggeration about the owners' complaints. It is convoluted, and 'shut up in the madhouse' does not clearly parse.

faults.quote: the way a man gets over the loss of a tooth, with a deal of fuss and then no more about it
faults.why: This is a new simile added to 'they'll get used to it'. It is acceptable as commentary, but it is unannounced and not in the notes, and it changes the register of the answer.

faults.quote: I judge a customer is mostly a customer afoot, anyhow, and can find a store as well on his own two legs as he ever could packed in a wagon.
faults.why: The writer's evidence, 'most people walk from the garage anyway', is garbled. The garage is lost. 'Packed in a wagon' is odd and does not carry the point that people already walk.

faults.quote: mostly a customer afoot
faults.why: The writer's point was that drivers already walk from the garage. Here it becomes a claim that customers are on foot generally, which would undercut the need for the parking complaint and contradict the first paragraph.

faults.quote: We ought to try it this summer, I reckon, and try it.
faults.why: The closing 'and try it' is a tautological, limp repeat. It reads like a garble rather than a deliberate rhythm.

faults.quote: their shops are doing better than ever they done before
faults.why: This is Huck's dialect, jarringly mixed with the more standard tone elsewhere. 'There's other towns' and 'ever they done' are inconsistent with 'ought to' and 'a deal of fuss'.

faults.quote: a body that wants to set a wagon down
faults.why: The Huck-style dialect mixed with Twain's essayistic narrator is a pastiche. The jokes are thin and lack a real Twain turn such as a straight-faced exaggeration with a reversal.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: The teller speaks his confidence in his own matters, as Huck does; it is a verdict on what the writer gave, not a new instrument of proof.
faults.why: The note is vague and does not name the actual changes. It describes 'I judge' only abstractly, and it ignores the wagon recast and the tooth simile, both of which are real changes.

faults.quote: The narrator underlines the one objection before answering it, in the voice's tall manner
faults.why: The note is inaccurate. The rewrite does not underline the objection beforehand. It is also placed under paragraph 2 and misses the other changes.

faults.quote: (no notes)
faults.why: Paragraphs 1 and 3 have no notes, though paragraph 1 makes the major cars-to-wagons change and adds a baby-carriage image. The notes also do not report that the answer was weakened.

faults.quote: But they'll get over it, the way a man gets over the loss of a tooth
faults.why: The outline said the strong half of the answer (walking from the garage) should move forward to sit beside the parking grievance. The rewrite does not do this and leaves it in place, garbled, so the stated plan was not carried out.

faults.quote: which lets the absurd comparison stand flat and do its own work
faults.why: The lesson praises the tooth simile as deadpan, but it is not very absurd and is not tied to the argument. The outline's advice was not applied, so the writer cannot see the structure lessons in the actual text.

judge.verdict: The rewrite puts the argument in a Huck-flavored mix and swaps cars for wagons, which muddles the modern setting. It garbles the 'walk from the garage' evidence into a different claim, and its notes and closing line are weak or inaccurate. The outline's promised restructuring is not performed.
