I think we should switch to a four-day week. People are burned out and our best engineer just quit. There are studies showing productivity stays the same or goes up. It would also help with hiring.

I know it's risky and clients might not like it. We could try it for three months and see.
rewrite:
I reckon we ought to drop one day and work four, instead of five. People are tired clean down to the bone, and our best engineer up and quit on us. There's studies that show the work don't slack off none for it—it stays the same, or it picks up. And it would make hiring a heap easier, too.

I know it's risky, and the clients might not take to it. But we could try it for three months, and see how it comes out.

rows.text: I reckon we ought to drop one day and work four, instead of five. People are tired clean down to the bone, and our best engineer up and quit on us. There's studies that show the work don't slack off none for it—it stays the same, or it picks up. And it would make hiring a heap easier, too.

notes.after: I reckon we ought to drop one day and work four, instead of five.

notes.text: The writer said 'burned out'; the voice gives it as the body's own saying, plain, rather than the modern word.
notes.after: people are tired clean down to the bone

rows.text: I know it's risky, and the clients might not take to it. But we could try it for three months, and see how it comes out.

notes.text: The writer said only "see"; "how it comes out" supplies a criterion of outcome the writer left open.
notes.after: But we could try it for three months, and see how it comes out.

lessons: Your passage is plain and short, but it is plain the way a memo is plain; Twain's talk is plain the way a man talking on a porch is plain, swinging and piling up and then dropping the point. I gave it a talking voice: "I reckon we ought to" instead of "I think we should," and "up and quit on us" where you had "just quit." Then I let the sentences run a little longer and land on the important word, like "it stays the same, or it picks up," so the reader hears the turn. Try, in your own voice, saying the thing as you would say it aloud to a friend, and let the sentence go where the talk wants to go before you set the period.

reading.kind: argument (a proposal, with an objection and a proposed trial)

outline.gist: We should switch to a four-day week.
Burned-out people; the best engineer just quit.
Studies show productivity holds or rises.
It would help with hiring.
It's risky; clients might not like it.
Try it for three months and see.

plan.gist: We should switch to a four-day week.
plan.why: A proposal goes first when the reader is busy and hostile; name the thing asked for before defending it, so every reason that follows has a hook to hang on and the reader knows what the evidence is for.

plan.gist: People are burned out and our best engineer just quit.
plan.why: Start with the fact the reader cannot argue with — something that has already happened in the reader's own shop. Twain makes his case out of what the audience can see for itself before he brings in any study; a close-to-home loss stings where a statistic only informs.

plan.gist: Studies show productivity stays the same or goes up.
plan.why: Bring the outside authority second, to back the local fact rather than replace it — a reader who has just felt the loss is ready to hear that it is not unique. One line, no piling on: a short list of proofs reads as confidence, a long one as worry.

plan.gist: It would also help with hiring.
plan.why: A second benefit, kept brief and after the first, because argument by accumulation is weaker than argument by strongest-point-first; it is the spare tire, not the engine.

plan.gist: I know it's risky and clients might not like it.
plan.why: Twain raises the other side's best shot himself and in plain words, because an objection stated by the proposer loses its teeth and the reader stops bracing to make it.

plan.gist: We could try it for three months and see.
plan.why: Answer the objection with a low-cost experiment, which shrinks the risk the objection named rather than denying it — the close should leave the reader with an action as small as the courage it takes, so refusal looks sillier than consent. Same order as the writer chose; only the objection now gets an answer aimed at it instead of sharing a paragraph with the trial that answers it.

faults.quote: People are tired clean down to the bone
faults.why: 'Burned out' (exhausted by work, a specific condition) is rendered as general tiredness, and the intensity is slightly raised. The notes treat this as a liberty but give a muddled reason.

faults.quote: and see how it comes out
faults.why: Adds 'how it comes out' to the writer's bare 'see'. The note flags it, but it is a small addition the rewrite did not need.

faults.quote: I reckon we ought to drop one day and work four, instead of five.
faults.why: The Twain-flavored vocabulary is only a light dialect sprinkle ('reckon', 'heap', 'up and quit'). There is no humor, no exaggeration, no deadpan irony, and no characteristic Twain turn. It reads like generic folksy Western speech, not Twain's essayistic voice.

faults.quote: the work don't slack off none for it
faults.why: The double negative and 'don't' with a singular subject is Huck Finn-style dialect. It is inconsistent with the proposal register and with Twain's own narrator voice, and sits oddly next to the more standard 'it would make hiring a heap easier'.

faults.quote: There's studies that show
faults.why: Ungrammatical agreement is dialect costume, mixed with the more formal 'it stays the same, or it picks up'.

faults.quote: cites The Innocents Abroad, ch. 4, ¶ 17
faults.why: This citation is dubious, probably fabricated, and not apt for a sentence of 'I reckon we ought to'. It does not name a real move.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: The writer said 'burned out'; the voice gives it as the body's own saying
faults.why: The note is vague, and 'tired clean down to the bone' isn't really the same claim. Only two or three moves are listed for the whole piece, and nothing explains the 'heap' or 'up and quit on us' choices.

faults.quote: Then I let the sentences run a little longer and land on the important word
faults.why: The rewrite's sentences are barely longer than the original, so the claim doesn't match the text. The lesson is generic ('say it aloud to a friend') and gives no concrete Twain technique such as understatement, a comic comparison, or the deadpan turn.

faults.quote: only the objection now gets an answer aimed at it instead of sharing a paragraph with the trial
faults.why: The outline claims a reordering or separation that the rewrite doesn't do. The objection and trial still share a paragraph, as in the original, so the outline describes a change that was not made.

judge.verdict: The content is faithfully kept and clear, but the voice is mostly a thin dialect coating with some ungrammatical mixing, and Twain's humor and cadence are absent. The notes include a doubtful citation and the lesson and outline claim changes the text doesn't show.

yours:
When Dana cancelled our dinner I wasn't upset at all. Honestly, I was relieved. I'd been dreading it all week, and I'm not proud of that.

I told her it was fine and we'd do it another time. I don't think we will.
rewrite:
When Dana cancelled our dinner I warn't upset, not a bit of it. I was relieved, I'll say it out plain: it's the truth. I'd been dreading it the whole week, and I'm not proud of that, neither.

I told her it was all right, and we'd do it another time, some time or other. But I don't think we will—I judge we'll never try it again, neither one of us being in any great sweat for it.

rows.text: When Dana cancelled our dinner I warn't upset, not a bit of it. I was relieved, I'll say it out plain: it's the truth. I'd been dreading it the whole week, and I'm not proud of that, neither.
I told her it was all right, and we'd do it another time, some time or other. But I don't think we will—I judge we'll never try it again, neither one of us being in any great sweat for it.

notes.text: The narrator turns his own verdict into a deadpan moral about the both of them, the way Huck sizes up a thing by how much sweat it would cost; it frames the writer's quiet certainty in the voice's own terms without adding a new incident.
notes.after: I judge we'll never try it again, neither one of us being in any great sweat for it.

notes.text: Adds an indefinite vagueness to the promised other time that the writer did not put there.
notes.after: some time or other

notes.text: “But” sets the last sentence against the promise in a way the writer leaves flat; the writer simply states it.
notes.after: But I don't think we will

lessons: The chief difference is that the writer's flat little sentences confess straight out, while Twain's narrator lets the voice carry the joke. \"I warn't upset, not a bit of it\" puts the denial in the vernacular so the relief feels like a man telling it aloud; and the last line lands the quiet certainty deadpan—\"I judge we'll never try it again, neither one of us being in any great sweat for it\"—so the reader feels the shrug instead of being told it. Practise turning a plain verdict into the teller's own sizing-up, as Huck does, and letting the short sentence arrive only at the end where it can land.

reading.kind: story (a short personal anecdote of a moment, told in the first person)

outline.gist: Dana cancelled; I wasn't upset — I was relieved.
I'd been dreading it all week, and I'm not proud of that.
I told her it was fine and we'd do it another time.
I don't think we will.

plan.gist: Dana cancelled; I wasn't upset — I was relieved.
plan.why: Keep it first. A confession of unexpected feeling is the hook: Twain opens flat and lets the reader think he agrees with them, so the plain 'I was relieved' lands as a shared secret and buys the right to the admission that follows.

plan.gist: I'd been dreading it all week, and I'm not proud of that.
plan.why: Keep it second. Twain always gives the reason after the surprising claim, never before, so the reader has already taken the narrator's side when the evidence arrives; and the self-blame is the Twain move of confessing before anyone can accuse.

plan.gist: I told her it was fine and we'd do it another time.
plan.why: Keep it third. It comes after the reader knows the truth, so the polite lie is seen as a lie, which is the whole joke; put it earlier and it would merely be courtesy.

plan.gist: I don't think we will.
plan.why: Keep it last, as Twain keeps his deadpan button: one short sentence after the longer ones, letting the reader supply the laugh. Do not add explanation — the flat understatement is the argument's close, and any gloss would explain the joke and kill it.

faults.quote: neither one of us being in any great sweat for it
faults.why: Adds a claim the writer never made: that Dana also does not want the dinner. The writer only speaks of their own relief and dread, so this invents Dana's feelings.

faults.quote: some time or other
faults.why: Adds vagueness to what the narrator said. The note admits this as a liberty, but it is an addition rather than commentary.

faults.quote: I judge we'll never try it again
faults.why: Strengthens the writer's mild 'I don't think we will' into 'never', and restates it in a second clause. The writer's doubt is hedged and quiet; this is harder and more explicit.

faults.quote: I warn't upset, not a bit of it. I was relieved, I'll say it out plain: it's the truth.
faults.why: Huck's dialect ('warn't', 'neither') is stuck onto a narrator who is not Huck. Twain's essayistic and anecdotal voice is not this dialect. The colon and 'it's the truth' sound like costume, and the explanation is forced.

faults.quote: I'm not proud of that, neither.
faults.why: 'Neither' is wrongly used here. The double negative needs a preceding negative to echo, and the construction is clumsy. It also jars with the standard 'I'd been dreading it the whole week' beside it.

faults.quote: in any great sweat for it
faults.why: 'In a sweat' means anxious or agitated, so 'in any great sweat for it' reads awkwardly for eagerness. The idiom is stretched.

faults.quote: But I don't think we will—I judge we'll never try it again, neither one of us being in any great sweat for it.
faults.why: The short deadpan closing sentence is turned into a long explained one. This is the very gloss the build analysis says would kill the joke, and the rewrite contradicts its own structure advice.

faults.quote:
Paragraph 1:
  (no notes)
faults.why: The first paragraph has large changes ('warn't', 'I'll say it out plain: it's the truth', 'neither') that go unreported.

faults.quote: “But” sets the last sentence against the promise in a way the writer leaves flat
faults.why: The writer's original has no 'But', so this is an added connective. The note is accurate, but the other notes are labelled vaguely as liberties and cite no real Twain source. The 'Huck' reference is also off for a Twain narrator.

faults.quote: Practise turning a plain verdict into the teller's own sizing-up, as Huck does, and letting the short sentence arrive only at the end where it can land.
faults.why: Contradicts the rewrite, which lengthens the last sentence. The lesson also gives the writer a vague tip tied to dialect rather than a reusable technique, and it endorses an addition (Dana's feelings) that the writer never made.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the core feelings but invents Dana's indifference, hardens 'I don't think we will' into 'never', and puts Huck-style dialect on a Twain narrator. The closing line is bloated against its own build advice, and the notes and lesson are thin and partly self-contradictory.
